entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12819"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen23830" type="x-p"/> Nahum means "consolation" and "vengeance"; symbolizing the "consolation" in the book for God's people, and the "vengeance" coming on their enemies. In the first chapter the two themes alternate; but as the prophet advances, vengeance on the capital of the Assyrian foe is the predominant topic. The name Capernaum, that is, "village of Nahum," seems to take its name from Nahum having resided in it, though born in Elkosh in the neighborhood. There is another Elkosh east of the Tigris, and north of Mosul, believed by Jewish pilgrims to be the birthplace and burial place of the prophet. But the book of Nahum in its allusions shows a particularity of acquaintance with Palestine (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.4">Na 1:4</reference>), and only a more general knowledge as to Nineveh (Na 2:4-6; 3:2, 3).<div eID="gen23830" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23829" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23831" type="x-p"/> His graphic description of Sennacherib and his army (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.9-Nah.1.12">Na 1:9-12</reference>) makes it not unlikely that he was in or near Jerusalem at the time: hence the number of phrases corresponding to those of Isaiah (compare <reference osisRef="Nah.1.8">Na 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Is 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.23">10:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.2.10">Na 2:10</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.24.1">Is 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.3">21:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.15">Na 1:15</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Is 52:7</reference>). The prophecy in <reference osisRef="Nah.1.14">Na 1:14</reference> probably refers to the murder of Sennacherib twenty years after his return from Palestine (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.38">Is 37:38</reference>). The date of his prophecies, thus, seems to be about the former years of Hezekiah. So Jerome thinks. He plainly writes while the Assyrian power was yet unbroken (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.12">Na 1:12</reference>; 2:11-13 <reference osisRef="Nah.3.15-Nah.3.17">Na 3:15-17</reference>). The correspondence between the sentiments of Nahum and those of Isaiah and Hezekiah, as recorded in Second Kings and Isaiah, proves the likelihood of Nahum's prophecies belonging to the time when Sennacherib was demanding the surrender of Jerusalem, and had not yet raised the siege (compare <reference osisRef="Nah.1.2">Na 1:2</reference>, &c., with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.14">2Ki 19:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.7">Na 1:7</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.22">2Ki 18:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.19">19:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.7">2Ch 32:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.9">Na 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">11</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.22">2Ki 19:22</reference>, 27, 28; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.14">Na 1:14</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.6">2Ki 19:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.15">Na 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2:1, 2</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.32">2Ki 19:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.33">33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.2.13">Na 2:13</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.22">2Ki 19:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.23">23</reference>). The historical data in the book itself are the humiliation of Israel and Judah by Assyria (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.2">Na 2:2</reference>); the invasion of Judah (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.9">Na 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">11</reference>); and the conquest of No-ammon, or Thebes, in Upper Egypt (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.8-Nah.3.10">Na 3:8-10</reference>). Tiglath-pileser and Shalmaneser had carried away Israel. The Jews were harassed by the Syrians, and impoverished by Ahaz' payments to Tiglath-pileser (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.1-2Chr.28.27">2Ch 28:1-27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.7.9">Is 7:9</reference>). Sargon, Shalmaneser's successor, after the reduction of Phoenicia by the latter, fearing lest Egypt should join Palestine against him, undertook an expedition to Africa (<reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Is 20:1-6</reference>), and took Thebes; the latter fact we know only from Nahum, but the success of the expedition in general is corroborated in <reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Is 20:1-6</reference>. Sennacherib, Sargon's successor, made the last Assyrian attempt against Judea, ending in the destruction of his army in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah (713-710 B.C.). As Nahum refers to this in part prophetically, in part as matter of history (Na 1:9-13; 2:13), he must have lived about 720-714 B.C., that is, almost a hundred years before the event foretold, namely, the overthrow of Nineveh by the joint forces of Cyaxares and Nabopolassar in the reign of Chyniladanus, 625 or 603 B.C.<div eID="gen23831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23832" type="x-p"/> The prophecy is remarkable for its unity of aim. He is seventh in point of date.<div eID="gen23833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23834" type="x-p"/> His style is clear, elegant, and forcible. Its most striking characteristic is the power of representing several phases of an idea in the briefest sentences, as in the majestic description of God in the commencement, the conquest of Nineveh, and the destruction of No-ammon [Eichorn]. De Wette calls attention to his variety of manner in presenting ideas, as marking great poetic talent. "Here there is something sonorous in his language there something murmuring; with both these alternates something that is soft, delicate, and melting, as the subject demands." Excepting two alleged Assyrian words (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.17">Na 3:17</reference>), English Version, "crowned," or princes, and English Version, "captains," or satraps (used by <reference osisRef="Jer.51.27">Jr 51:27</reference>), the language is pure. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12820"/><div sID="gen23836" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12820"/><hi type="bold">2. jealous--</hi>In this there is sternness, yet tender affection. We are jealous only of those we love: a husband, of a wife; a king, of his subjects' loyalty. God is jealous of men because He loves them. God will not bear a rival in His claims on them. His burning jealousy for His own wounded honor and their love, as much as His justice, accounts for all His fearful judgments: the flood, the destruction of Jerusalem, that of Nineveh. His jealousy will not admit of His friends being oppressed, and their enemies flourishing (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Ex 20:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.22">1Co 16:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2Co 11:2</reference>). Burning zeal enters into the idea in "jealous" here (compare <reference osisRef="Num.25.11">Nu 25:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.25.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.10">1Ki 19:10</reference>).<div eID="gen23836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord revengeth ... Lord revengeth--</hi>The repetition of the incommunicable name Jehovah, and of His revenging, gives an awful solemnity to the introduction.<div eID="gen23837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23838" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">furious--</hi>literally, "a master of fury." So a master of the tongue, that is, "eloquent." "One who, if He pleases, can most readily give effect to His fury" [Grotius]. Nahum has in view the provocation to fury given to God by the Assyrians, after having carried away the ten tribes, now proceeding to invade Judea under Hezekiah.<div eID="gen23838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23839" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reserveth wrath for his enemies--</hi>reserves it against His own appointed time (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.9">2Pe 2:9</reference>). After long waiting for their repentance in vain, at length punishing them. A wrong estimate of Jehovah is formed from His suspending punishment: it is not that He is insensible or dilatory, but He reserves wrath for His own fit time. In the case of the penitent, He does not reserve or retain His anger (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.9">Psa 103:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.5">Jr 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">Mi 7:18</reference>). <div eID="gen23839" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12828"/><div sID="gen23858" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12828"/><hi type="bold">10. while they are folden together as thorns--</hi>literally, "to the same degree as thorns" (compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.27">1Ch 4:27</reference>, Margin). As thorns, so folded together and entangled that they cannot be loosed asunder without trouble, are thrown by the husbandmen all in a mass into the fire, so the Assyrians shall all be given together to destruction. Compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6">2Sa 23:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.7">7</reference>, where also "thorns" are the image of the wicked. As this image represents the speediness of their destruction in a mass, so that of "drunkards," their rushing as it were of their own accord into it; for drunkards fall down without any one pushing them [Kimchi]. Calvin explains, Although ye be dangerous to touch as thorns (that is, full of rage and violence), yet the Lord can easily consume you. But "although" will hardly apply to the next clause. English Version and Kimchi, therefore, are to be preferred. The comparison to drunkards is appropriate. For drunkards, though exulting and bold, are weak and easily thrown down by even a finger touching them. So the insolent self-confidence of the Assyrians shall precipitate their overthrow by God. The Hebrew is "soaked," or "drunken as with their own wine." Their drunken revelries are perhaps alluded to, during which the foe (according to Diodorus Siculus [2]) broke into their city, and Sardanapalus burned his palace; though the main and ultimate destruction of Nineveh referred to by Nahum was long subsequent to that under Sardanapalus. <div eID="gen23858" type="x-p"/>

navigation_sections.content_plain: INTRODUCTION Nahum means "consolation" and "vengeance"; symbolizing the "consolation" in the book for God's people, and the "vengeance" coming on their enemies. In the first chapter the two themes alternate; but as the prophet advances, vengeance on the capital of the Assyrian foe is the predominant topic. He is called "the Elkoshite" ( Na 1:1 ), from Elkosh, or Elkesi, a village of Galilee, pointed out to Jerome [Preface in Nahum] as a place of note among the Jews, having traces of ancient buildings. The name Capernaum, that is, "village of Nahum," seems to take its name from Nahum having resided in it, though born in Elkosh in the neighborhood. There is another Elkosh east of the Tigris, and north of Mosul, believed by Jewish pilgrims to be the birthplace and burial place of the prophet. But the book of Nahum in its allusions shows a particularity of acquaintance with Palestine ( Na 1:4 ), and only a more general knowledge as to Nineveh (Na 2:4-6; 3:2, 3). As Nahum refers to this in part prophetically, in part as matter of history (Na 1:9-13; 2:13), he must have lived about 720-714 B.C., that is, almost a hundred years before the event foretold, namely, the overthrow of Nineveh by the joint forces of Cyaxares and Nabopolassar in the reign of Chyniladanus, 625 or 603 B.C. Nahum's object was to inspire his countrymen, the Jews, with the assurance that, however alarming their position might seem, exposed to the attacks of the mighty Assyrian, who had already carried away the ten tribes, yet that not only should the Assyrian (Sennacherib) fail in his attack on Jerusalem, but Nineveh, his own capital, be taken and his empire overthrown; and this, not by an arbitrary exercise of Jehovah's power, but for the iniquities of the city and its people. Its most striking characteristic is the power of representing several phases of an idea in the briefest sentences, as in the majestic description of God in the commencement, the conquest of Nineveh, and the destruction of No-ammon [Eichorn]. De Wette calls attention to his variety of manner in presenting ideas, as marking great poetic talent. "Here there is something sonorous in his language there something murmuring; with both these alternates something that is soft, delicate, and melting, as the subject demands." Excepting two alleged Assyrian words ( Na 3:17 ), English Version, "crowned," or princes, and English Version, "captains," or satraps (used by Jr 51:27 ), the language is pure. These two, doubtless, came to be known in Judea from the intercourse with Assyria in the eighth and seventh centuries B.C.
